headline: First Jobs, Fake Essays and Golden Cats for Sale
teaser: Is AI sawing off the first rung of the career ladder? Can software prove who wrote an essay? And could selling rare cats as pets ever protect them?

articles.title: Fewer Rungs on the Ladder: Is AI Closing the Door to First Jobs?
articles.dek: A new report says AI-heavy industries are hiring fewer beginners. Is AI really to blame, and who should rebuild the first rung of the career ladder?

sources.name: NPR Morning Edition via WUSF, 23 Nov 2026
Burning Glass Institute & RAISE US, "Fewer Rungs, New Bridges"

paras: For generations, the path into a professional career has looked like a ladder. Young people started on the bottom rung, doing routine tasks such as entering data, answering customer emails or drafting simple reports, and gradually climbed toward more complex and better-paid work. A new report suggests that artificial intelligence may be quietly sawing off that first rung. Published by the Burning Glass Institute, a labor-market research group, and RAISE US, a workforce organization, the study is titled "Fewer Rungs, New Bridges," and its findings have prompted a lively debate about what AI means for the next generation of workers.

The report focuses on four industries that have adopted AI tools especially quickly: finance, insurance, information and professional services. In August 2026, these sectors employed 31.9 million people. That sounds like a large number, but it is about 1.5 million fewer than would be expected if employment had continued to grow at the pace it followed between 2005 and 2019. Crucially, the authors argue that this gap is not mainly the result of dramatic layoffs. "The missing workers aren't being laid off," they write; "they're simply not being hired in the first place." In other words, companies are not necessarily firing existing staff; they are opening fewer doors to newcomers.

The evidence for this is clearest at the entry level. In the industries that use AI most heavily, the share of job postings open to candidates with three years of experience or less was between 3 and 8 percent below its recent average in the year ending in June 2026. Office and administrative support jobs, which have long served as a starting point for workers without specialized training, fell by 780,000 between 2023 and 2025. The logic is easy to follow: the routine tasks that once justified hiring a junior employee are exactly the tasks that AI systems can now perform cheaply and quickly.

Yet the picture is not simply one of destruction. Within the occupations most exposed to AI, the report found that jobs likely to be automated lost about 820,000 positions, while jobs in which AI assists rather than replaces workers gained roughly 1.4 million. Moreover, across the economy as a whole, the share of postings aimed at entry-level candidates has remained largely unchanged. The authors themselves treat AI as only one of several likely causes of the hiring gap, alongside offshoring and other technologies. Skeptics therefore caution against blaming a single technology for complex economic shifts; slower hiring may also reflect high interest rates and uncertainty about the economy.

Even so, the burden of change appears to fall unevenly. Workers without a bachelor's degree hold 64 percent of all jobs but 80 percent of the jobs most likely to be automated. This matters because entry-level roles have traditionally been a route upward for such workers: according to the report, more than four in five established advancement pathways that begin in jobs requiring no degree lead to positions that typically do require one. If the bottom rung disappears, the authors warn, the entire ladder may become harder to climb, and inequality could widen.

The report's title also points to a possible solution: "new bridges." AI, after all, can teach as well as replace. Studying 2,741 career moves into occupations facing worker shortages, the researchers estimated that AI tools could help newcomers close about 31 percent of the skills gap between their old and new jobs. However, in another 46 percent of these transitions, AI mainly helped people who were already skilled, which could make it even harder for beginners to compete. Gina Raimondo, a former US Commerce Secretary who co-chairs RAISE US, called the findings a "wake-up call for leaders from Washington to Silicon Valley."

What should those leaders do? Some argue that companies have a responsibility to keep training junior staff, even when AI could do their tasks more cheaply, because today's beginners are tomorrow's experienced managers. Others believe the solution lies in education: schools and universities should teach students to work alongside AI, so that graduates arrive with skills that machines cannot easily copy. For students preparing to enter the workforce, the message is neither panic nor complacency. The first rung of the ladder may be changing shape, but those who learn to use AI as a tool, rather than compete with it, may still find a way up.

keySentences.text: A new report suggests that artificial intelligence may be quietly sawing off that first rung.
keySentences.note: The ladder metaphor turns the report into one clear claim: AI may be removing the starting point of careers. Main-idea sentences like this guide the whole passage.

keySentences.text: Crucially, the authors argue that this gap is not mainly the result of dramatic layoffs.
keySentences.note: "Crucially" signals the most important detail: the problem is fewer hires, not more firings. TOEFL factual questions often test this kind of distinction.

keySentences.text: Yet the picture is not simply one of destruction.
keySentences.note: "Yet" marks a turn in the argument. Expect the paragraph to give the other side, here the jobs that AI helps create.

keySentences.text: Skeptics therefore caution against blaming a single technology for complex economic shifts; slower hiring may also reflect high interest rates and uncertainty about the economy.
keySentences.note: "may also reflect" shows that AI is not the only possible cause. Noticing hedges helps you avoid answer choices that are too extreme.

keySentences.text: If the bottom rung disappears, the authors warn, the entire ladder may become harder to climb, and inequality could widen.
keySentences.note: A clear if-then chain: losing first jobs leads to fewer chances to rise, which could increase inequality.

keySentences.text: For students preparing to enter the workforce, the message is neither panic nor complacency.
keySentences.note: The author's balanced conclusion. "neither ... nor" rejects two extremes, a pattern often tested in inference questions.

write.p:
Dr. Chen: A new report suggests that AI-heavy industries are hiring fewer beginners, and some experts say the first rung of the career ladder is disappearing. Who should be mainly responsible for helping young people get their first jobs in the age of AI: companies, or schools and universities? Why?
Lily: "Companies. If they stop training juniors today, there will be no experienced staff tomorrow. Firms that profit from AI should invest some of those savings in apprenticeships."
Tom: "I think schools must lead. Companies exist to make money, so we can't rely on them. Schools should teach students to work with AI so they are ready from day one."
steps: State who you think should be mainly responsible.
Respond to Lily or Tom and add a new reason.
Support it with an example or a fact from the article.

articles.title: Catch Me If You Can: The Arms Race Between AI Writers and AI Detectors
articles.dek: A new detector can learn as it goes, but AI-writing tools keep changing. Should schools trust software to judge whether students cheated?
paras: Ever since chatbots learned to produce fluent essays in seconds, teachers have faced an uncomfortable question: how can they tell whether a student wrote an assignment or simply asked a machine to write it? Many schools have turned to AI text detectors, software that estimates how likely it is that a passage was generated by a large language model. A new study from researchers at MIT and Cornell Tech, however, suggests that these tools are far less reliable than many users assume, and that keeping them accurate may require a fundamentally different approach.

The problem lies in what computer scientists call a "moving target." A detector is trained on examples of human and AI writing that exist at a particular moment. But both kinds of writing keep changing. New chatbots appear regularly, and each produces text with a slightly different style. Meanwhile, a whole industry of so-called "humanizers" has emerged: tools that rewrite AI-generated text so that it slips past detectors. "After the company releases a model, a bunch of 'humanizers' pop up to try to beat it," explained Kevin Ren, a graduate student at Cornell Tech and the study's lead author. Even human writing drifts over time, as new words, topics and habits spread.

To measure how serious the problem is, the team tested detectors on AI text that had been deliberately disguised. The results were striking. One commercial detector caught only about 27 percent of the disguised passages. A tool that misses most of the cases it was designed to catch offers little protection, and it may give teachers a false sense of security.

The researchers' proposed solution is a technique called test-time adaptation. Normally, updating a detector means collecting large amounts of new, labeled data, in which every example is marked as human or AI, and then retraining the model from scratch, a slow and expensive process. With test-time adaptation, the detector instead adjusts its internal settings continuously, learning from the new, unlabeled text it encounters while it is being used. Using this method, the detector caught more than 93 percent of the disguised text. When the team simulated the gradual drift of human writing over time, the adaptive detector was 85 percent accurate, compared with 73 percent for traditional methods. The work will be presented at NeurIPS, one of the world's leading conferences on artificial intelligence.

Manish Raghavan, an MIT professor and co-author, said the results show that test-time adaptation can make detectors "much more robust." Yet the researchers are notably cautious about what their work means. As language models become more natural and human-written text becomes harder to verify, adaptation may not always succeed. "It isn't entirely clear if this will be a solvable problem," Raghavan admitted. The study's figures also come from the researchers' own datasets, so they will need to be tested independently.

This caution matters because detectors can fail in two directions. Besides missing AI-generated text, they can wrongly flag genuine human writing, an error known as a false positive. In 2023, researchers at Stanford University found that seven popular detectors, on average, misclassified more than half of a set of TOEFL essays written by non-native English speakers as AI-generated, apparently because these writers tend to use simpler and more predictable vocabulary. For a student, being falsely accused of cheating can damage grades, reputations and trust, even if the accusation is later withdrawn.

As a result, educators are divided. Some argue that detectors, if used carefully, remain a useful deterrent: students who know their work may be checked are less tempted to cheat. Others believe that schools should stop treating writing as a product to be policed and instead redesign assignments, for example by asking students to write in class, submit drafts or explain their reasoning aloud. MIT's report on the study goes further, suggesting that teachers may want to think twice before putting all their trust in a detector's verdict.

Ultimately, the contest between AI writers and AI detectors may resemble an arms race with no finish line: each improvement in detection invites a new method of evasion. If that is true, the most reliable evidence of learning may not come from software at all, but from the conversations, drafts and thinking that only a real student can produce.

write.p:
Dr. Patel: Researchers have found that AI text detectors can be fooled by "humanizer" tools and can also wrongly flag real student writing. Should schools use AI detectors to decide whether students have cheated? Why or why not?

articles.title: Pets or Protection? A Plan to Breed Rare Wild Cats for Sale
articles.dek: An Indonesian company wants permission to breed Asian golden cats for the global pet trade. Could a legal market protect wild cats, or put them at greater risk?
paras: Deep in the forests of South and Southeast Asia lives a cat that few people have ever seen. The Asian golden cat, which weighs between 9 and 16 kilograms, is considerably larger than a house cat, and its coat can range from bright gold to cinnamon, grey or even black. It is shy, mostly solitary and rarely photographed. Now this elusive animal is at the centre of an international controversy, after an Indonesian company asked for permission to breed it commercially and sell it to pet owners around the world.

The species' range stretches from eastern Nepal and north-eastern India through Myanmar, Thailand and southern China to Malaysia and the Indonesian island of Sumatra. It is listed as vulnerable by the International Union for Conservation of Nature (IUCN), and an estimated 7,000 individuals remain in the wild. Their numbers are falling mainly because forests are being cleared and because the cats are poached for their skins and bones; in some markets, their bones are sold as substitutes for tiger parts in traditional medicine. The species is also listed in Appendix I of the Convention on International Trade in Endangered Species (CITES), which bans international commercial trade in wild-caught animals.

There is, however, an important exception. Animals bred in captivity at facilities registered with CITES can be traded legally with the proper export permits. This is the door that the company, PT Alam Nusantara Jayatama, hopes to open. According to documents submitted by Indonesia's Ministry of Forestry, the firm began breeding in 2013 with four legally acquired wild-caught cats, and by 2025 it reported 36 animals across three generations. In August, the CITES Secretariat notified member countries of the application, giving them until November 10 to object. If the facility is registered, it would become the first in the world to breed Asian golden cats commercially for the international pet market.

Supporters of commercial captive breeding often use a simple economic argument. If buyers can obtain legally bred animals, the reasoning goes, they will have less reason to buy animals taken from the wild, and pressure on wild populations will ease. In theory, a legal supply could undercut the black market. Neither the company nor its owner responded to journalists' questions, however, so the firm's own case has not been explained publicly.

Conservation experts are deeply skeptical. Chris Shepherd of the Center for Biological Diversity, a US-based environmental group, described the plan as "very suspicious" and argued that commercial captive breeding rarely reduces demand for wild animals and often hinders conservation. One concern is that a legal trade can provide cover for an illegal one: once golden cats are openly sold, it may be hard for officials to tell whether a particular animal was bred in captivity or trapped in a forest. A legal market could also make owning rare cats seem fashionable, increasing overall demand.

Others question whether the breeding figures are realistic. Mike Brocklehurst, a carnivore specialist who once ran a conservation breeding programme at Melbourne Zoo, said the cats are "super challenging to breed," adding that males in captivity sometimes kill females when the two are introduced. In his view, the company's reported success probably depends on removing kittens from their mothers at an early age and raising them by hand, a method that allows mothers to breed again sooner.

Animal welfare is a further worry. Sandra Reichler, a mammal curator at Heidelberg Zoo who leads the European zoo association's breeding programme for the species, warned that separating kittens from their mothers too early can cause lasting behavioural problems. She also noted that the company's enclosures measure about 9 square metres, while European zoos recommend a minimum of 150 square metres. A wild cat that naturally roams a large forest territory may suffer in a space smaller than a typical bedroom.

The case raises a broader question that goes far beyond one species: can markets protect wildlife, or do they inevitably put it at greater risk? Some conservationists believe that carefully regulated trade can reduce poaching, as has been argued for certain farmed crocodiles. Others insist that wild animals should not be pets at all, however they are bred. As CITES considers the application, the fate of the Asian golden cat may depend on which of these views prevails.

uoe.title: Use of English · C1 Advanced
uoe.intro: Cambridge C1 Advanced (CAE) style practice built on today's three stories: grammar, vocabulary, collocations and word formation.

parts.title: Multiple-choice cloze
parts.task: Read the text and decide which answer (A, B, C or D) best fits each gap.
parts.text: For decades, entry-level jobs have been where young professionals learn the {1}. Routine tasks allowed newcomers to {2} experience while learning from senior colleagues. Now, however, a growing number of employers are {3} advantage of artificial intelligence to handle such work. According to a recent report, the problem is not that staff are being dismissed {4} masse, but that fewer beginners are being taken on in the first place. Some economists warn that this trend could {5} a whole generation behind. Others are less pessimistic, {6} out that AI is also creating roles in which people work alongside machines. It goes without {7} that graduates will need new skills, and those who can make the most of AI tools are likely to stand a far better {8} of climbing the career ladder.

items.why: "Learn the ropes" is an idiom meaning to learn the basic skills of a new job. The other nouns do not form this idiom.
"Gain experience" is the natural collocation. You win a prize, score a goal and reach a target, but you gain experience.
"Take advantage of something" means to use it to benefit yourself. The other verbs do not combine with "advantage of".
"En masse" (from French) means all together, in large numbers. "In masse", "on masse" and "at masse" are not English expressions.
"Leave someone behind" means to cause them to fall behind others. "Let" and "put" don't form this meaning with "behind", and "drop behind" is used without an object.
Only "point" combines with "out" to mean "mention a fact" (point out that...). "Show", "note" and "indicate" are not followed by "out" here.
"It goes without saying that..." means something is so obvious that it hardly needs to be said.
"Stand a (good/better) chance of doing something" is a fixed collocation. We don't say "stand a better hope/opportunity/possibility".

parts.title: Open cloze
parts.task: Think of the word which best fits each gap. Use only ONE word in each gap.
parts.text: Teachers have long worried about students handing in work that is not {9} own. With the arrival of chatbots, this concern has grown, and many schools now rely {10} software to spot AI-generated essays. Yet such tools are far from perfect. Not {11} do they miss a large proportion of disguised texts, but they also sometimes accuse innocent students. Researchers have found that writers {12} first language is not English are especially likely to be flagged. {13} a result, some educators argue that detectors should be used, if at {14}, only as a starting point for a conversation. {15} approach a school chooses, most experts agree on one point: no detector should be trusted completely, {16} matter how advanced it appears.

items.why: "Work that is not their own" = work they did not do themselves. The possessive "their" refers back to "students".
The verb "rely" is followed by "on" (or the more formal "upon").
"Not only do they..., but they also..." uses inversion after the negative phrase "Not only".
"Whose" shows possession in a relative clause: writers whose first language is not English.
"As a result" introduces a consequence of the problem just described.
"If at all" means "if they are used in any way", suggesting they may not be used at all.
"Whichever/Whatever approach a school chooses" = it doesn't matter which approach; the main clause is true in every case.
"No matter how advanced it appears" = however advanced it appears.

parts.title: Word formation
parts.task: Use the word in capitals to form a word that fits in the gap.
parts.text: The Asian golden cat is a remarkably {17} animal that few people have ever seen in the wild. Its long-term {18} is threatened by poaching and by the {19} of the forests in which it lives. Now a plan to breed the cat commercially for the pet trade has proved highly {20}. Critics argue that such schemes are {21} to reduce poaching, and may even help to disguise the {22} trade in wild-caught animals. Zoo experts also question the {23} of the company's breeding figures, and they stress that keeping a forest animal in a tiny cage is simply {24}.

items.why: An adjective is needed after "remarkably": elude (verb) → elusive (hard to find).
After the possessive "Its long-term" we need a noun: survive → survival.
"the ___ of the forests" needs a noun: destroy → destruction (note the spelling change).
"proved highly ___" needs an adjective: controversy → controversial.
The critics doubt the schemes will work, so we need a negative adjective: unlikely to reduce.
A legal trade could hide the trade in wild-caught animals, which is not legal: legal → illegal (il- before l).
"question the ___ of" needs a noun: rely → reliable → reliability.
The experts disapprove, so we need a negative adjective: accept → acceptable → unacceptable.

parts.title: Key word transformation
parts.task: Complete the second sentence so that it has a similar meaning to the first, using the word given. Do not change the word given. Use between three and six words, including the word given.

items.why: "People say that X is ..." becomes the passive "X is said to be ...". Answer: is said to be (4 words).

items.s1: The company did not answer any of the journalists' questions.
items.why: "did not answer" becomes "made no response to". Answer: no response to (any of) (3–5 words).

items.s1: Experts doubt that commercial breeding will reduce poaching.
items.post: whether commercial breeding will reduce poaching.
items.why: The verb "doubt" becomes the noun phrase "have doubts about". Answer: have doubts about (3 words).
